extraction.name: CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography
extraction.description: CADS is an open-source framework for whole-body CT segmentation comprising a large-scale dataset of 22,022 CT volumes with complete annotations for 167 anatomical structures. The dataset aggregates CT scans from over 40 diverse sources spanning 16 countries and more than 100 imaging facilities, collected between 2007 and 2024. It includes data from public archives (TCIA, Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges), specialized annotation collections, and newly contributed images (484 head CTs and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans). The framework also includes the CADS-model, a robust fully automated segmentation model suite trained on the CADS-dataset, and a 3D Slicer plugin for clinical deployment.
extraction.license: Multiple licenses depending on source dataset; users must comply with individual licenses and terms of use for each source dataset.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The CADS-dataset aggregates CT scans from three main sources: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator (1,203 annotated volumes), NLST (7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans); (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI) and focused research studies (Han-Seg, SAROS, TCIA oncology studies); and (3) newly contributed images comprising 484 anonymized head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar. The collection spans more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries. Selection criteria focused on CT scans covering key anatomical regions including brain, head-and-neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, and femur. Approximately 79% of the initial collection did not include any manual annotations.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 21% of the 22,022 CT volumes (4,695 volumes) contain partial annotations from public sources, with annotations typically confined to a single organ system. Approximately 79% of the initial collection does not include any manual annotations. Some structures have limited training data (e.g., buccal mucosa appears in less than 1,000 scans with only 30 ground-truth annotations).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: CT volumes from over 40 diverse sources including: public archives (TCIA, Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges), large-scale datasets (TotalSegmentator, NLST, CT-RATE, AbdomenCT-1K, SAROS), specialized research datasets (Han-Seg, VISCERAL, KiTS, LiTS, BTCV, CHAOS, VerSe, and others), and newly acquired hospital data (484 head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CTs from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar).
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: For the SAROS dataset, which provides sparse slice-based 2D annotations with labels available only on selected slices, interpolation between annotated slices was performed to create dense 3D per-slice annotations required for volumetric training.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A multi-stage annotation pipeline was applied: (1) pseudo-labeling using specialized models for nine anatomical groups to propagate annotations across unlabeled scans; (2) shape-based quality control using neural implicit functions to detect and exclude outlier pseudo-labels (lowest-scoring 10% excluded); (3) multi-strategy label generation through ensemble selection of three model flavors (GT-flavor, Pseudo-flavor, Shape-flavor) with statistical ranking; (4) assembly of final labels with progressive merging order based on label reliability, with original GT annotations taking highest priority. Rib segmentation refinement was performed using vesselFM for costovertebral joint retrieval and connected components analysis for fragmentation correction. Head region pseudo-labels were refined to mitigate hallucinations using brain voxel count thresholding and bounding box cropping.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-step preprocessing pipeline was applied: (1) reorientation of all images to standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention; (2) resampling to uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution; (3) simplification of original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear. For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (sigma=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions. Intensity scaling from 5th to 95th percentiles to range [0,1] with clipping for contrast enhancement was applied during model training.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were created through multiple approaches: (1) Original ground truth annotations from existing public datasets (e.g., TotalSegmentator with 104 structures, Han-Seg for head-and-neck OARs, SAROS for broad body context structures); (2) Manual annotations by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (JCP) on the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset for 10 additional structures including spinal canal, larynx, heart chambers, and other structures critical for radiotherapy planning; (3) Registration-derived annotations for brain structures by registering Han-Seg CT scans with the SimNIBS MRI atlas using ANTS non-rigid transformation; (4) Pseudo-labels generated by specialized nnU-Net models for each of nine anatomical groups across all 22,022 CT volumes; (5) Expert-verified subset created for benchmarking by reviewing 65 test images from TotalSegmentator dataset, with in-house medical professionals examining pre-corrected labels and classifying each annotation as reliable or unreliable. For the real-world hospital cohort, reference annotation masks were either generated using MIM software and validated by medical doctors, or directly contoured by radiation oncologists following standard clinical protocols.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: MIM software (for University Hospital Zurich cohort annotations); 3D Slicer (for visualization and clinical use); nnU-Net framework for automated pseudo-label generation
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A systematic flavor selection process was used to determine the best annotation source for each structure: statistical tests (Shapiro-Wilk for normality, Levene's for variance equality, followed by ANOVA/Welch's ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis with post-hoc Tukey's HSD or Dunn's test) compared three model flavors using Dice Similarity Coefficient as primary metric and HD95 as secondary metric. Shape-based outlier detection using neural implicit functions identified and excluded the lowest-scoring 10% of pseudo-labels. Expert review of TotalSegmentator ground truth labels identified recurrent annotation errors including mislabeling between adjacent structures, missing segments, over-segmentation, and boundary inaccuracies. A radiation oncologist (5.5 years in practice) conducted systematic expert review of CADS-model segmentations on the clinical cohort, evaluating three representative cases per structure around the median Dice score.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Variable; 167 anatomical structures annotated per fully annotated volume; partially annotated volumes contain annotations for one or more structures. Only 21% of volumes (4,695 of 22,022) contain any original annotations.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Three in-house medical research assistants and one radiation oncologist (Jan C. Peeken) contributed manual annotations. Expert review for clinical validation was conducted by an experienced radiation oncologist with 5.5 years in practice. Label quality review was contributed by Nikhil Mirajkar and Saad Khalid (Labelata GmbH, Zurich, Switzerland).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net framework (version 2.5.1) for specialized model training and pseudo-label generation; neural implicit functions (auto-decoder based on implicit neural representations) for shape-based quality control; vesselFM (foundation model for 3D blood vessel segmentation) for rib costovertebral joint retrieval; ANTS (Advanced Normalization Tools) for non-rigid registration of brain structure annotations; SimNIBS MRI atlas for brain structure annotation registration; PyTorch (version 2.5.1) with CUDA 12.4; Seg-metrics and surface-distance packages for evaluation; TPTBox Python library for postprocessing
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The CADS-dataset is publicly accessible via https://huggingface.co/datasets/mrmrx/CADS-dataset. Trained models and codebase are publicly available at https://github.com/murong-xu/CADS. A 3D Slicer plugin is available at https://github.com/murong-xu/SlicerCADS. No explicit versioning or deprecation policy is stated in the paper.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes CT scans from patients with various pathological conditions. For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter was applied to facial regions to obscure identity. All newly acquired head and abdominal CT scans are anonymized. The study received ethical approval from the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at Istanbul Medipol University (E-10840098-772.02-6841, 27/10/2023) for the 484 head CT scans, and from the Ethics Committee of the Technical University of Munich (27/19 S-SR) for the 586 abdominal CT scans. Patient demographics include age (head CT patients aged ≥18 years) and various pathological conditions.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: CADS aims to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. Clinical applications include: streamlining radiation therapy treatment planning through rapid organ delineation; enabling automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes in diagnostic radiology; facilitating large-scale population studies. The 3D Slicer plugin with SNOMED-CT terminology integration supports integration into existing healthcare infrastructures. By making the dataset, models, and tools publicly available, the framework aims to reduce barriers for healthcare practitioners without technical expertise.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The exclusion strategy in shape-based quality assessment may eliminate cases involving pathological conditions with atypical anatomical variations, potentially limiting the model's ability to learn clinically important edge scenarios. The dataset's data-centric approach aims to mitigate class imbalance and potential biases through multi-source integration. Some structures have limited representation (e.g., uppermost cervical vertebrae C1-C5 appear less frequently). Annotation quality issues were identified in existing widely-used public datasets, particularly in complex structures like ribs and vertebrae. Facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: (1) Exclusion of pathological cases with atypical anatomical variations due to shape-based quality control; (2) Coverage limited to head to knees, excluding hands and feet; (3) Brain mask includes all central nervous components within the skull; (4) Optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; (5) Heart segmentation omits superior portions; (6) Rectum appears shorter than anatomical extent; (7) Trachea limited to air content without surrounding tracheal wall; (8) Vena cava needs more precise delineation; (9) Facial features are anonymized; (10) Some structures have limited training data (e.g., buccal mucosa in less than 1,000 scans); (11) Very small organs (volumes below 0.5 mL) are challenging due to CT resolution limits and partial volume effects; (12) Vascular structures are often absent due to annotation complexity.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use cases include: (1) Training whole-body CT segmentation models; (2) Testing and validation of segmentation algorithms across 18 public datasets and independent clinical cohorts; (3) Radiation therapy treatment planning (organ-at-risk delineation); (4) Anatomical landmark detection; (5) Cross-modality registration (CT-MRI fusion, PET-CT alignment); (6) Anatomy-guided image synthesis and reconstruction; (7) Longitudinal organ tracking; (8) Personalized anatomical modeling; (9) Large-scale population studies; (10) Body composition analysis. The dataset is intended for academic research use, with users required to comply with individual source dataset licenses.
